questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Expressions Using the Double-Angle Formula for Sine
questions.worked_solution:
In this case, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,⇒\,\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta 
$$

 

Letting $\theta =4x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡8x & =\operatorname{sin}⁡4x\operatorname{cos}⁡4x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x\operatorname{cos}⁡4x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡8x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{cos}⁡8x{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =-\frac{1}{16}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{16}(1-1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡2x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Rearranging the above formula, we get

$$
\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (2x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (2x-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)\text{d}x \\  & =2(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})-\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)+C \\  & ={x}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Letting $\theta =\frac{5x}{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡5x & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5x}{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5x}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5x}{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5x}{2})\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /10}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡5x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /10}\operatorname{sin}⁡5x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡5x]}_{0}^{\pi /10} \\  & =-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{cos}⁡5x\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /10} \\  & =-\frac{1}{10}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\cdot \frac{\pi }{10})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\cdot 0)] \\  & =-\frac{1}{10}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)] \\  & =-\frac{1}{10}\cdot [0-1] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}.\end{aligned}

questions.worked_solution:
Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta 
$$

Letting $\theta =\frac{3x}{2},$ we get

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)={cos}^{2}\,(\frac{3x}{2})-{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{3x}{2}).
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}({cos}^{2}\,(\frac{3x}{2})-{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{3x}{2}))\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /6} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{6})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area $A$ of the region in the $xy$-plane that is bounded by the curve $y=-5{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{2})+5{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{2})+4x+7,$ the $x$-axis and the lines $x=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $x=0,$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the region is given by

$$
A={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}(-5{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{2})+5{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{2})+4x+7)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To calculate this integral, we use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x={cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x
$$

We can rewrite the above formula as

$$
-5\operatorname{cos}⁡x=-5{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{2})+5{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{2}).
$$

Hence, the area of the region is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}(-5{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{2})+5{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{2})+4x+7)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}(-5\operatorname{cos}⁡x+4x+7)\,\text{d}x \\  & =(-5\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2{x}^{2}+7x)\,{|}_{-\pi /2}^{0} \\  & =[-5\operatorname{sin}⁡0+2(0)^{2}+7\cdot 0]-[-5\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})+2{(-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}+7(-\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =0-[5+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{2}-\frac{7\pi }{2}] \\  & =-5-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{2}+\frac{7\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The area of the region is given by

$$
A={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(3{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{2})-3{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{2})+2x+1)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To calculate this integral, we use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x={cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x
$$

We can rewrite the above formula as

$$
3\operatorname{cos}⁡x=3{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{2})-3{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{2}).
$$

Hence, the area of the region is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(3{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{2})-3{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{2})+2x+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(3\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2x+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =(3\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{x}^{2}+x)\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =[3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+(\pi )^{2}+\pi ]-[3\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+(0)^{2}+0] \\  & =[0+{\pi }^{2}+\pi ]-0 \\  & ={\pi }^{2}+\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Recall  ${cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x=1,$ so we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}3{sin}^{2}⁡x+7{cos}^{2}⁡x & =3{sin}^{2}⁡x+3{cos}^{2}⁡x+4{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =3({sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x)+4{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =3+4{cos}^{2}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡x$ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=2{cos}^{2}⁡x-1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡x=\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1).
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(3+4{cos}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}[3+\frac{4}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1)]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(5+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)\text{d}x \\  & ={(5x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =[5\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})]-[5\cdot 0+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot 0)] \\  & =[\frac{5\pi }{4}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})]-[0+\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)] \\  & =[\frac{5\pi }{4}+1]-[0+0] \\  & =\frac{5\pi +4}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

The area of the region is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}A={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}(2{cos}^{2}⁡x+x-1)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate this integral, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡x$ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=2{cos}^{2}⁡x-1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡x=\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1).
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}(2{cos}^{2}⁡x+x-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}[(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1)+x-1]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+x)\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi )+\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{3\pi }{2})}^{2}]-[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}) \\  & ={\pi }^{2}.\end{aligned}

$$
2{cos}^{2}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1.

Substituting this into the expression $4{cos}^{2}⁡x-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x,$ we get

$$
4{cos}^{2}⁡x-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=2(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=2.

$$

questions.worked_solution:
Recall  ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,$ so letting $\theta =3x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡(3x)-4{sin}^{2}⁡(3x) & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡(3x)-4{sin}^{2}⁡(3x) \\  & =1-5{sin}^{2}⁡(3x).\end{aligned}
$$

Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${sin}^{2}$ term: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta 
$$

We can rearrange the above formula as

$$
\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

Letting $\theta =3x,$ we have

$$
\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x))={sin}^{2}⁡(3x).
$$

We can now integrate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}(1-5{sin}^{2}⁡(3x))\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}(1-5\cdot \frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)))\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}(\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)-\frac{3}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{5}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)-\frac{3}{2}x)\,|}_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3} \\  & =[\frac{5}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\cdot \frac{5\pi }{3})-\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{5\pi }{3}]-[\frac{5}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\cdot \frac{\pi }{3})-\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{\pi }{3}] \\  & =[0-\frac{5\pi }{2}]-[0-\frac{\pi }{2}] \\  & =-2\pi \end{aligned}
$$

The area of the region bounded by the curve $y=2x-{sin}^{2}⁡x+\frac{1}{2},$ the $x$-axis and the lines $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ and $x=\frac{3\pi }{4}$ is

$$
A={\int }_{\pi /4}^{3\pi /4}(2x-{sin}^{2}⁡x+\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${sin}^{2}$ term: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=1-2{sin}^{2}⁡x
$$

We can rearrange the above formula as

$$
\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-1)=-{sin}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Hence, the area of the region is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{3\pi /4}(2x-{sin}^{2}⁡x+\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{3\pi /4}(2x+\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-1)+\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{3\pi /4}(2x+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)\,|}_{\pi /4}^{3\pi /4} \\  & =(\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{16}+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{3\pi }{4}))-(\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{16}+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})) \\  & =(\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{16}-\frac{1}{4})-(\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{16}+\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}-1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${sin}^{2}$ term: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

We can rearrange the above formula as

$$
1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

Letting $\theta =\frac{x}{4},$ we have

$$
1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{x}{4}).
$$

We can now integrate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }[2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{x}{4})-1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})]\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }[1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})-1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\text{d}x \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2}){|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Using the Squared Sine Variant of the Cosine Double-Angle Formula
questions.worked_solution:
Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${sin}^{2}$ term: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta 
$$

We can rearrange the above formula as

$$
\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

Letting $\theta =\frac{x}{6}$, we have

$$
4{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{6})=2(1-cos\,(\frac{x}{3})).
$$

We can now integrate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\,\,[4{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{6})-2+4cos\,(\frac{x}{3})]dx & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\,\,[2-2cos\,(\frac{x}{3})-2+4cos\,(\frac{x}{3})]dx \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}2cos\,(\frac{x}{3})\,dx \\  & =6sin\,(\frac{x}{3}){|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =6[sin\,(\frac{\pi }{2})-sin\,(\frac{\pi }{6})] \\  & =6(1-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Integrating Expressions Using the Double-Angle Formula for Sine
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
In this case, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\sin {2\theta} =2\sin \theta \cos \theta\quad\Rightarrow\quad \dfrac{1}{2}\sin(2\theta) = \sin{\theta}\cos{\theta}.
$$

 

Letting $\theta= \dfrac{x}{2},$ we get

$$
\eqalign{
\dfrac{1}{2} \sin \left(2\cdot \dfrac{x}{2} \right) &= \sin \left(\dfrac{x}{2} \right)\cos\left( \dfrac{x}{2}\right)\[5pt]
\dfrac{1}{2}\sin x	&= \sin \left( \dfrac{x}{2}\right) \cos  \left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right).
  }
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\eqalign{
		\int \sin \left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) \cos \left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) \, \textrm{d}x&=\int \dfrac{1}{2}\sin {x} \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt]
								&=\dfrac{1}{2} \int \sin {x} \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt]
								&=\dfrac{1}{2} \left( - \cos {x}\right )+C \[5pt]
								&=-\dfrac{1}{2} \cos {x}+C.	
	}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Integrating Expressions Using the Double-Angle Formula for Cosine
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We can use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
\cos^2\theta -\sin^2\theta=\cos 2\theta.
$$

Letting $\theta = 3x$ gives

$$
\cos^2 3x - \sin^2 3x = \cos 6x,
$$

and therefore,

$$
\eqalign{
		{\int} \left(\cos^2 3x - \sin^2 3x\right ) \, \textrm{d}x&=\int  \cos 6x\, \textrm{d}x\
								&=\dfrac{1}{6}\sin6x+ C.\
                                                                
	}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Integrating Using the Squared Cosine Variant of the Cosine Double-Angle Formula
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the $\cos^2{x}$ term, given by

$$
\cos{2x} =2\cos^2 x -1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
\cos^2 x = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\cos 2x +1 \right).
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\eqalign{
		\int \cos^2 x \, \textrm{d}x&=\int  \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\cos 2x +1 \right) \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt]
								&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int ( \cos {2x} +1) \textrm{d}x\[5pt]
                                                                 &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\sin {2x} +x\right) + C\[5pt]
								&= \dfrac{1}{4}\sin {2x} +\dfrac{1}{2}x + C.
								
	}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the $\sin^2$ term: 

$$
\cos {2\theta}=1-2\sin^2\theta.
$$

We can rearrange the above formula as

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}\left(1-\cos {2\theta} \right )=\sin^2\theta.
$$

Letting $\theta = 3x$, we have

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}\left(1-\cos {6x} \right )=\sin^2(3x).
$$

We can now integrate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {sin}^{2}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡6x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int (1-\operatorname{cos}⁡6x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(x-\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡6x)+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡6x+C.\end{aligned}
$$
